speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: asked	the Minister for Education (Schools) whether the Ministry has plans to further reduce the number of primary and secondary schools and junior colleges (JCs) in view of a smaller student population as compared to when the schools were first started or built.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: asked	the Minister for Education (Schools) why the Ministry did not consider shelving the establishment of the new Eunoia Junior College and convert one or more junior colleges out of the four that are to be discontinued to offer the same educational programme planned for Eunoia Junior College.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: asked	the Minister for Education (Schools) (a) whether the reduced supply of junior college places following the merger of JCs will result in higher aggregate scores for JC admission; and (b) whether the Ministry was expecting an increase in admissions when Eunoia Junior College was set up.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: asked	the Minister for Education (Schools) whether junior college mergers will continue beyond 2018 in light of falling birth rates.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: In planning for schools, our priorities are to meet the demand for school places at both the national and local levels and ensure accessibility to students based on proximity to housing developments and public transport.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: At the national level, the fall in live births over the past two decades has led to a corresponding decline in the demand for school places.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This demographic wave is felt across all levels of our school system.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Earlier this year, MOE announced the mergers of 14 more pairs of schools in 2019.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We recognise that school mergers are painful for students, staff and alumni, but they are necessary.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Without mergers, some schools will be facing such low enrolment that they will not be able to provide our students with the array of subject combinations, co-curricular activities (CCAs) and enrichment programmes that they deserve.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The 32 mergers which have been announced since 2015 will bring down our overall school places.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Patrick Tay and Mr Seah Kian Peng asked if there would be further school mergers, given the falling cohort sizes.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We want to give some time for things to settle down and monitor choice and enrolment patterns before making any further decisions.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Our priority for the next few years is to support our schools, staff and students as we adjust to these mergers.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: However, in the longer term, with the demographic shifts both at the national and localised levels, we cannot rule out the need for more mergers in the next decade, difficult though they may be.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Four pairs of junior colleges (JCs) will be merged for the first time in 2019.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If MOE does not take any action now, several of our JCs would find themselves with JC1 intake of below 400, less than half of the typical 800.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Some would even struggle to fill 200 places.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: When this happens, the educational experience of the students enrolled in these JCs will be severely compromised.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We decided that it is better to plan for the mergers now to ensure a smooth transition for the merging schools and affected students and teachers.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We settled on the eventual JC merger pairs after taking into consideration a few factors, especially student choice and the enrolment patterns of the JCs.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We also considered geographical spread of the merged pairs and compatibility of merger partners.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: After the mergers, we would preserve good geographical distribution of Government non-IP JCs, with one each in the West, North, Northeast and East regions.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The mergers involve the eight Government non-Integrated Programme (IP) JCs as mergers involving Government-aided schools pose significant issues and additional challenges due to their governance framework.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: MOE considered different options before making the difficult decision to merge schools.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: One was to retain schools even when enrolment has fallen very low and bring together students from various schools and run programmes at the cluster or regional level.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: However, we decided against it as staff and students will face operational challenges, such as timetabling constraints, and travelling between different schools for activities would add to their commute time.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Our students' educational experience and their experience of school life would inevitably be compromised.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We also believe that there is value in enabling students to immerse themselves in their schools.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: That is what builds a sense of belonging and school spirit.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Leon Perera suggested that instead of merging JCs, we allow a reduction in class sizes in those JCs with low enrolment.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We are merging schools to ensure a good range of programmes for our students in schools that would otherwise face low enrolment.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: MOE takes a needs-based resourcing approach for teacher resourcing, targeting additional support at students with greater learning needs by reducing class sizes in a selective manner, so as to improve our educational outcomes across different schools and student profiles.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have been able to do this due to our steadily improving teacher-to-student ratios, which are now comparable to that of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We believe that this approach in reducing class size is more targeted and sustainable and can be applied across all schools based on needs, rather than just the schools with low enrolment.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The sites of the merged schools in 2019 are chosen based on a number of factors, including the accessibility to public transport and the quality of school infrastructure, which includes the age of buildings and facilities available.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: In addition, for the JC mergers, the selected merged sites took into consideration the desire for us to have a good spread and distribution of JCs across the island.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Schools' heritage and identities are valuable aspects of our students' experience.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The names of the merged schools have not been decided.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: In naming the merged schools, MOE will consider the schools' history and heritage, stakeholders' interests and the sentiments of all schools involved.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Similar to primary and secondary school mergers, the merged JC will comprise a significant proportion of staff from both JCs.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will retain the special programmes and events, plus the signature CCAs of both JCs, so that the heritage of the merged JC is enriched from merging aspects of both colleges.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Over the years, MOE has engaged school leaders and many educators on the issue of falling cohort sizes and the rationale for school mergers at various MOE engagement platforms.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: As Members would appreciate, the issue of the actual school merger is very emotive and we need to approach this matter with care.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is not a matter that we can do extensive pre-announcement engagements without causing unnecessary anxiety.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Our engagements are focused on the post-announcement phase, targeting key areas of concerns for staff and students, such as support during the transition and preservation of their school heritage.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I understand that some parents and students are concerned that fewer JCs would mean stiffer competition for places.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: A related question is how the eventual JC cut-off points for the 2018 Joint Admission Exercise would change with the JC mergers.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: They vary from year to year depending on students' choices.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We do not know how students' choices may change with the announcement of JC mergers.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For this reason, I am unable to give specific answers to Mr Zaqy Mohamad's nor Mr Leon Perera's questions as to whether we will see higher aggregate scores for JC admissions or specific percentages following the mergers.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: With the change in the 2018 JC landscape, variations in cut-off points may be slightly more than in previous years.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Our educators, as well as Education and Career Guidance Counsellors, will continue to guide our students in selecting their post-secondary pathways based on their strengths, aspirations and interests.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Pritam Singh asked why we chose to set up Eunoia Junior College (EJC), and if we had anticipated falling JC cohort sizes in the coming years.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: MOE had decided to set up various new schools in 2010, namely, Crest, Spectra, as well as EJC, as part of our efforts to provide more options in our education landscape, and better meet our students' diverse aspirations and educational needs.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This was even though we were aware of the falling cohort sizes in the coming years.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Crest and Spectra were specially established to offer a special Normal (Technical) curriculum to cater to secondary school students who are more suited for the applied learning track.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: In the same vein, we set up the new EJC to cater to students who would benefit from the IP pathway at three secondary schools − Catholic High, Convent of the Holy Infant Jesus (CHIJ) St Nicholas Girls' and Singapore Chinese Girls'.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We started the new IP pathway in 2004, with the intention that this would, over time, admit up to 10% of the Primary School Leaving Examination (PSLE) cohort, and the IP pathway has been valued by students.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The extension of IP to these three schools and the announcement of EJC in 2010 were part of this planned IP expansion.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The suitability of a JC to partner its feeder secondary schools to offer IP is an important consideration to ensure that the programme offered will be meaningful for the students.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: At that time, there was no suitable JC to partner these three secondary schools.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: EJC was thus set up to leverage the strengths of the partner secondary schools and to add diversity to the JC landscape.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Like Mr Desmond Choo, MOE recognises that school mergers are unsettling for school staff.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: In the case of teachers, this sometimes involves redeployment to another level, for example, from secondary school to primary school, or JC to secondary or primary school.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There are also areas of needs in MOE Headquarters, such as developing resources for information and communications technology learning for our students, and other vacancies where teachers could contribute.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: MOE takes great care in managing staff matters in school mergers.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We work closely with school leaders and support them in engaging affected staff.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Staff are engaged on the deployment plans and manpower needs for the merged schools.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: They are also informed of the redeployment plans and support available to them.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Many of these conversations take place on a one-to-one basis.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Thereafter, staff are given time to explore options they are interested in through our internal posting exercise.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: MOE will also assist staff who need additional support during the redeployment process.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: MOE will provide the necessary training for teachers who will be redeployed to levels they have not taught before.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The training includes bridging courses to equip them with the necessary pedagogical skills and content knowledge to teach at the redeployed level.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Apart from deepening their understanding of the different learning profiles of the students they will teach, these bridging courses will also help teachers understand their students' different social and emotional needs, and how they can foster strong teacher-student rapport to help them better support these students in their learning.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: These teachers will also have the opportunity to be attached to their new schools before their formal postings begin.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: After they have been posted, MOE will continue to support these teachers through regular engagement sessions.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Apart from providing teachers with the requisite training, we recognise that redeployed teachers will also need personal time and space to adapt to their new environment.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I understand that the process of school mergers is a difficult and challenging one for the schools and all stakeholders involved.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We are making every effort to ensure that the transition will be a smooth one.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We value our students' learning experience and their attachment to our schools.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Thus, we are also committed to continue the rich heritage and history of our schools through the cohorts of students to come.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I just have two supplementary questions, as well as clarifications and suggestions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I am glad to hear that none of the teaching and non-teaching staff would be made redundant and retrenched.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: However, as we know, because of such rationalisation, there will be transfers of teachers, including non-teaching staff, for example, the administrative staff.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I say this because I speak on behalf of the four teachers' unions as well as our public sector unions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: There is general concern how they will be helped because different schools have different cultures, geographically as well as whether they are primary and secondary schools, or JCs.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: They will need professional training and assistance to make the transition work.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The Member's point about engaging the union is an apt and appropriate one.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, I hope the Member appreciates that we made the announcements and began engagements as soon as we were able to, with some confidence that there was clarity over the decisions that we were going to go forward with.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But the larger point that we do have to make sure that we work well with the teachers' unions and have good labour relations in this aspect is very important.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The first question is that if geographical location is one of the criteria that was taken into account, did the Ministry consider that in closing Serangoon Junior College, potential students residing in the northeast areas like Sengkang, Punggol and Hougang, would be affected, that is, they would have to travel to a college that is further away?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second supplementary question is that there is some talk that only the Government-funded, non-IP, non-Mission, non-affiliated JCs are being merged.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we look at the list of schools to be closed, that hypothesis does not seem entirely baseless.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What is the Senior Minister of State's comment on what I would say is a popular view that is being taken?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The third supplementary question is that if low enrolment is a criterion, last year's Straits Times reported about the growing popularity of a few JCs, namely, Meridian JC, Nanyang JC and Serangoon JC.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Was this taken into account for this particular criterion of low enrolment?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does the Ministry not agree that by choosing to close down these schools, they would, to some extent, have undone some of the hard work that the principals and staff had put in?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Could I just ask who were the stakeholders from the affected JCs who were consulted?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: With respect to the first and the third questions, the geographical considerations and enrolment were taken into account.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, for both dimensions − the enrolment as well as the geographical location − we can find examples where it is not ideal.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There is no nice or ideal solution to this.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is painful to close a school, merge a school or relocate a school.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Yes, there would be some students who will end up having a slightly longer commute.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is not the only factor, but geographical considerations were taken into account.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The point the Member made was that we were undoing the work of the staff to build up a JC.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I think whether you are a low-enrolment school or a high-enrolment school, you would feel that your work has been undone.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Ultimately, that work and the values and the effort rest in the professionals who are involved.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The key part of a school is the teachers, staff and the ethos and values they bring.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: They are staying within our system; we are not losing them.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: As we merge these schools, these professionals who are part of our education landscape, the key part of our education landscape, the work that they have done in developing their profession and developing their schools, will be preserved within our system because they are all being retained within our system or have the opportunity to be retained within our system.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: As for the issue of the Government non-IP schools, I think I have addressed that in my response initially that it is correct that the mergers involve the Government non-IP JCs, and there are a couple of reasons.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I am just trying to find the paragraph, so I can refer the Member to it.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If you have a Government-aided school versus a Government school, the governance framework is different.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If you are trying to merge two schools with two very different governance frameworks, there are additional challenges − not impossible but it adds an added layer of complexity and difficulty that we felt was not needed at this point in time, that we could do it without having to engage in an even more difficult exercise.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Was there an additional point about that that the Member had?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I mean, we do acknowledge that it is so, and I hope I have explained why it is so.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Is there a concern by the Ministry that there will be a further decline in the number of JC places, in the sense that they are talking about future graduate workforce in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The second question is whether the Senior Minister of State would say that the JC experience, in terms of infrastructure and environment, has not really changed compared to, say, competition, such as polytechnic places where today, there is a lot more vibrancy in terms of marketing and the variety of courses being made available.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If you go to the polytechnics, for example, many of the students I spoke to and asked, "Why did you choose polytechnics over JCs?", for example, they would say, "You go to a JC, you see classrooms and classrooms and not much more, whereas if you go to the polytechnic, you will see labs, very interesting things".

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, the experience also matters in terms of the erosion of JC places.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would the Ministry be reviewing that because there is value to a JC education?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would not having changed this environment and experience result in further erosion of students taking the JC pathway, given that you also have more competition for students today, with regard to whether it is the International Baccalaureate (IB), IP or polytechnics?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: In absolute numbers, it may change but in terms of proportions, the pathways are there.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We anticipate that, likely, the proportions will remain about the same going forward.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is hard to say, but that is our anticipation of the future.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The Member brought up a very important point about the methodology of teaching in JCs.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If I understand that correctly, that perhaps there are aspects of the curricular experience or the student experience in our JCs which are different from what someone might experience at the polytechnics.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have increasing diversity in the post-secondary education landscape.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For a student to be offered more choice where the choice is not merely about the certification pathway or the accreditation pathway, or the academic process that they are going through, but the holistic student experience they may have, is a good thing.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If there is an opportunity for the JCs to think about how they can improve their provision of a student experience because of competition for the students to go to alternative pathways, that can also only be a good thing to improve our education landscape.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I do not think the changes in enrolment numbers, the falling birth cohort and our need for mergers of institutions would change any of these.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is a natural outcome of the increasing diversity that we want to have and that we are developing within our education space.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Why was it not possible for MOE to transfer staff and to provide resources to support the IP Programme to existing JCs, especially since the Ministry was aware of falling cohort sizes in 2010?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This would have allowed the long heritage of some JCs which are going to be closed shortly, as announced this year, to continue to grow and thrive?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There was no singular reason why that was not done.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And later on, as part of the programme, we wanted to ensure that geographical distribution and access to public transport, the changes where housing is going to be going forward, where the population shifts are going, are considered.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, there is no single neat reason why one particular route was not taken.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It was really an overall approach, and judgement was made that this was perhaps the best way to go forward to try to deal with the problem, which is a painful problem.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: One consideration is the pain and the distress the alumni feel.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is not something to be trivialised or ignored, and it is not something that MOE was unaware of.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But MOE has to balance that with how we can best serve the next generation.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Whether it is the geographical distribution, the enrolment, the emotional distress of the alumni, we cannot allow any single factor to override completely what should be our prime concern, which is, how to develop an education system that is going to best serve the next generation, looking forward to the future.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There are unknowns but that is how we have to approach this problem.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We acknowledge the problems and the distress that it has caused and we are trying our best to minimise them.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My question would be in terms of the longer-term planning protocols and processes within MOE.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Are there any learnings that have been drawn from this?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Clearly, falling birth rates would have been foreseeable a very long time ago because these are patterns that do not tend to fluctuate too much year by year.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Nevertheless, capacity did increase over the last decade.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I think the Senior Minister of State did acknowledge that in the context of discussing CCA clustering, increasing travel times does diminish the quality of the student experience.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would the Senior Minister of State acknowledge that this is in some sense penalising those students who opt for the JC path but perform less well academically, and what measures are going to be taken to manage that?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thirdly, my understanding is that at the time when the JC mergers were announced, MOE was in the process of implementing a new curriculum in JCs and this was the curriculum that MOE invested in, bringing teachers in to train the JC teachers on this new curriculum.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There was a period when the teachers would have to review the curriculum, revise and test their teaching materials, get feedback from the teaching process and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My question is just on the timing of the announcement.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would the timing not have been better if it had been either before or after the implementation of this new curriculum, which, it is my understanding, is currently in process?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If I could address the last question, we are looking at all staff, different groups of staff and different types of challenges.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We are looking at all staff to ensure that they have opportunities.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The third question is about the timing of the announcement, the curriculum review and training of teachers.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Yes, there were announcements of specifics for the JC curriculum review.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But the reality is that curriculum review, pedagogical development and professional training are ongoing all the time.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There is always going to be tweaks to our system.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There is always going to be new courses and new skills to be developed.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There is never going to be a good time.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There is never going to be the equivalent of a "Now it is school holidays and we can clean the canteen".

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: In terms of our education system, this ongoing professional review is constant.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will always find something happening and something going on.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, we had to make the choice for the timing of this in terms of how far ahead we had to plan for birth cohorts, at which point we were going to have an enrolment that was so low that a JC was not going to be able to run a viable programme with CCAs and performing arts and so forth, and the academic curriculum.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, that is fundamentally what determines the timing, not anything else.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: As for the cut-off points, and how it may affect the students who are, perhaps, not performing so well, this will vary over time.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: As schools merge and other schools see changes in capacity, the cut-off point required to get into a given JC may change.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It depends on some degree of competitiveness amongst the student cohort and it depends on the choices that students make.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There is no deliberate attempt to penalise anybody here.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There is no deliberate attempt to put the burden of these school mergers on a particular segment of our population.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: What will happen over time is that the cut-off points and the choices that students make will change.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And, really, there is no way to accurately plan or predict that except to say, on the whole, every JC-eligible student will have a place in the system.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The first question that the Member brought up was about lessons that have been learnt.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is going to be a dynamic process.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The changes in birth cohort, the changes in where population lives and what we do in our education system, will require a dynamic process.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We are not going to turn around and say that was the wrong thing to do at that time because now we are reducing places and merging schools.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: That was what we needed to do then, and this is what we need to do now.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We do have to take a dynamic approach.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The forward projection of the birth cohort is unknown.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
